turns.prompt_text: Do you know those like piles of TVs or they have like a collage of many monitors and TVs? I see them sometimes in different shows.
turns.response_html:
Absolutely, those are iconic. Whether they are neatly stacked in a grid or piled up like a mountain of glowing glass, they usually go by names like Video Walls, CRT Stacks, or Monitor Collages.

Depending on who you ask—an artist, a film director, or a technician—those piles of screens represent very different things.

1. The Artistic Origin: Nam June Paik

If you’re looking for the "grandfather" of this look, it’s the Korean-American artist Nam June Paik. In the 1960s and 70s, he began using television sets as a medium for high art.

  • The Perspective: For Paik, these weren't just screens; they were "electronic wallpaper."
  • The Famous Work: His piece Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii is a massive neon-lit map of the U.S. filled with 336 televisions. It was a commentary on how media would eventually connect (and overwhelm) us all.

2. The "Mastermind" Trope in Film & TV

In shows and movies, a wall of monitors is shorthand for information power.

  • The Surveillance Expert: Think of the "man in the chair" or a hacker like in Swordfish. Having ten screens doesn't necessarily make you faster, but it looks like you’re processing more reality than a normal person.
  • The God-Like Villain: Ozymandias in Watchmen or The Architect in The Matrix Reloaded are classic examples. Sitting in front of a dozen screens suggests they are watching everything at once, detached from the "single-screen" life of a regular human.

3. The Cyberpunk & Retro-Tech Aesthetic

There is a specific subculture (often linked to Cyberpunk or Vaporwave) that views these piles of old CRT (Cathode Ray Tube) TVs as a form of "low-life, high-tech" beauty.

  • The Appeal: Collectors love the warm hum, the static, and the physical bulk of old TVs. In a world of thin, flat OLEDs, a "pile" of heavy, glowing boxes feels tactile and industrial.
  • The Vibe: It represents a future that never quite happened—where technology is messy, wires are everywhere, and the "digital" is still a physical, heavy object.

4. The Engineering Reality: Broadcast and Security

In the professional world, these are purely functional.

  • Broadcast Control Rooms: Directors need to see every camera angle simultaneously to "cut" a live show.
  • Security Hubs: In a casino or a massive data center, the "collage" is a necessity for situational awareness.

Why do they "pile" them instead of just using one big screen?

Even though we now have massive 98-inch 8K displays, directors still use the "multi-screen collage" because it creates visual rhythm. A single large screen is a window; a hundred small screens is a pattern. It feels more chaotic, more "hacker-ish," and frankly, much cooler on camera.

Do you remember a specific show where you saw one? Usually, the "vibe" of the room tells you exactly what kind of character lives there.

turns.prompt_text: I've seen them used in Cowboy Bebop and Judge Dredd and on a few other podcasts.
turns.response_html:
Those specific examples—Cowboy Bebop and Judge Dredd—really lean into the "Information Overload" and "Surveillance State" vibes of those worlds. When you see them in podcasts today, it’s usually a deliberate nod to that 80s/90s Cyberpunk or Retro-Futurist aesthetic.

Here is how those specific "piles" function in the things you mentioned:

1. Cowboy Bebop: The "Brain Scratch" Tower

In the episode Brain Scratch (Session 23), you see a massive, jagged mountain of old televisions.

  • The Character: This is the primary visual for Dr. Londes, the leader of a cult called "Scratch" that wants people to upload their souls to the internet.
  • The Symbolism: The show uses that pile of TVs to represent a "New Religion." Londes argues that television is a device that "bombards people with information until they lose their sense of reality." By appearing on a stack of flickering CRTs, he’s literally manifesting as a god made of media and static.

2. Judge Dredd: The Hall of Justice Control Room

In both the comics and the 2012 film Dredd, the monitor walls are a tool of Totalitarian Control.

  • The Setting: Inside the Grand Hall of Justice, "Tech-Judges" sit in front of massive grids of monitors showing feeds from every corner of Mega-City One.
  • The Function: It represents the "all-seeing eye" of the law. In a city of 800 million people, the only way to maintain order is through a literal collage of surveillance. Unlike the "messy" pile in Bebop, the Dredd walls are usually sterile, grid-like, and overwhelming—designed to make the individual feel small and watched.

3. The Podcast "Set" Trend

You’ve likely seen this on podcasts because it has become a popular way to make a digital space feel "physical" and "authentic."

  • The "Hacker" Aesthetic: Podcasts like The WAN Show (Linus Tech Tips) or high-production video essayists like Nerd City use walls of screens or stacks of old monitors to create a "Command Center" vibe. It suggests the host is "plugged in" to the pulse of the internet.
  • The Lo-Fi/Retro Vibe: For many gaming or tech podcasts (like The Retro Hour or various lo-fi streams), a stack of old CRT TVs provides a warm, nostalgic glow that looks better on camera than a flat LED screen. It gives the set "texture" and a sense of history.

Why do they keep showing up?

Whether it’s a cult leader in an anime or a guy talking about tech on YouTube, the TV Collage serves two main purposes:

  1. Complexity: It visually signals that "a lot is happening here."
  2. The "Ghost in the Machine": There’s something eerie and powerful about a human face being split across multiple different screens. It makes the person look like they are part of the technology itself.

Do the ones you see on podcasts usually look like the "messy pile" (like in Bebop) or the "neat grid" (like in Dredd)? That usually tells you if they’re going for a "renegade/hacker" vibe or a "professional/high-tech" look.

2. Google Lens: The "Sourcing" Phase

Once you find a photo you love, switch to Google Lens.

  • How it works: You can upload an image of a setup, and it will identify the specific monitor stands, arms, or even the desk and monitor models.
  • Why use it: Since you mentioned using "many cheap monitors," you can use Lens to find older, used monitor models that people are successfully using in these stacks. It’s also the best tool for finding the exact heavy-duty mounting hardware required to support a "piled" monitor wall.

3. NotebookLM: The "Synthesizing" Phase

Once you have gathered articles, manuals, and technical specs, NotebookLM is your final stop.

  • How it works: You can feed it PDFs of monitor manuals, Reddit threads about daisy-chaining displays, and blog posts about cable management.
  • Why use it: In an office with a high number of screens, the technical side—like how many outputs your computer supports or how to manage the massive power load—becomes complex. NotebookLM can "read" all those sources and summarize the technical feasibility for you.

Practical Tips for the "Mixed Monitor" Setup:

  • The "Anchor" Display: For a project like this, keep the high-quality monitors directly in your line of sight for primary work. Use the cheaper, older screens for "passive" info like terminal logs, music players, or monitoring tools.
  • Color Matching: If you have screens from different brands, they will all have different "whites." A common trick is to set the entire "wall" to a monochromatic color scheme or use them primarily for text-heavy windows to hide the difference in panel quality.
  • Mounting Strategy: In an apartment, you’ll likely want "freestanding" multi-monitor mounts rather than wall-mounted ones to avoid wall damage. Look for "triple monitor stands" or "quad monitor stands" with a heavy base.
